title: Big O Notation for Beginners
description: What Big O means, the common complexity classes, and a practical method for reading JavaScript and naming its time and space complexity.

blocks.content:
Big O notation is one of the **most important concepts in Data Structures & Algorithms (DSA) tests**.

It tells you **how the amount of work an algorithm does grows as the input size `n` grows**.

blocks.text: If my input becomes 10× bigger, how much more work will my algorithm have to do?

blocks.body: Big O is about **growth rate**, not exact milliseconds. Two algorithms can both be O(n) and still differ in real-world speed — but the O tells you how they scale when `n` gets large.

items.label: How do you determine Big O?

blocks.content:
You'll encounter these constantly in coding interviews and tests:

| Big O | Name | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **O(1)** | Constant | Access an array element |
| **O(log n)** | Logarithmic | Binary search |
| **O(n)** | Linear | Loop through an array |
| **O(n log n)** | Linearithmic | Merge sort |
| **O(n²)** | Quadratic | Nested loops |
| **O(2ⁿ)** | Exponential | Some recursive problems |
| **O(n!)** | Factorial | Permutations |

Generally:

**O(1) → O(log n) → O(n) → O(n log n) → O(n²) → O(2ⁿ) → O(n!)**

The further right you go, the worse the algorithm scales.
2. How do you determine Big O?
The easiest approach starts with one question.

blocks.code: n = number of elements in the input

blocks.content: This is probably the **most important skill for DSA tests**.

The loop executes approximately `n` times.

Therefore: **O(n)**

First loop: `n`

Second loop: `n`

Total: `n + n = 2n`

We drop constants: `O(2n) → O(n)`

So the answer is **O(n)**.

The outer loop runs `n` times.

For every iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs `n` times.

Therefore: `n × n = n²`

So: **O(n²)**

This is an extremely common interview question.

First part: **O(n)**

Second part: **O(n²)**

Together: `O(n + n²)`

We keep only the **dominant term**: **O(n²)**

blocks.body: **Rule:** Drop everything except the fastest-growing term.

blocks.content:
Technically that's `3n`, but Big O is still **O(n)**. We don't care about the `3`.

Similarly, `O(100n)` is still **O(n)**.
This is another very important pattern. Look at:

Suppose `n = 16`.

Iterations:

```text
16
8
4
2
1
```

Only 4 iterations.

For `n = 1,000,000`, it's only around 20 iterations.

That's because we're **cutting the problem in half each time**.

Therefore: **O(log n)**

Binary search is the classic example.
When looking at code, ask: **"How does the loop variable change?"

blocks.code: for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)
for (let i = 1; i < n; i *= 2)

blocks.content: 10. An important trap: loops don't always mean O(n)

You might think **O(n²)**.

But the inner loop always runs **10 times**, regardless of `n`.

Therefore: `10 × n = O(n)`

So this is **O(n)**.

blocks.body: Only count loops whose bound depends on `n`. A fixed `10` (or any constant) does not change the Big O class.

blocks.content:
The inner loop isn't always `n` iterations.

It runs approximately:

`n + (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1`

which equals approximately `n² / 2`.

Drop the constant: **O(n²)**
12. Big O isn't just about loops
You also need to understand the complexity of **data structure operations**.

`arr[index]` is usually **O(1)**.

But `arr.includes(value)` may check every element: **O(n)**.

And `arr.unshift(value)` can require shifting existing elements: **O(n)**.

`map.get(key)` — average **O(1)**

`map.set(key, value)` — average **O(1)**

This is why hash maps are extremely important in DSA.

A balanced BST lookup is typically **O(log n)**.

But an unbalanced tree can degrade to **O(n)**.

You'll eventually see two different questions:

> What is the **time complexity**?

> What is the **space complexity**?

**Time:** O(n) — we process every element.

**Space:** O(n) — `result` grows with the input.

So you'd answer:

```text
Time:  O(n)
Space: O(n)
```
When you get a DSA question, use this mental checklist:

blocks.code:
1. What is n?
       ↓
2. How many times does the code execute?
       ↓
3. Are loops sequential or nested?
       ↓
4. Does anything divide the problem?
       ↓
5. Is there recursion?
       ↓
6. What is the dominant term?
       ↓
7. Drop constants
       ↓
8. Answer Big O

blocks.content:
Think:

```text
n = arr.length

outer loop → n
inner loop → roughly n

n × n

→ O(n²)
```

Therefore: **Time = O(n²)**

And because it doesn't create another data structure proportional to `n`: **Space = O(1)**

Don't try to memorize hundreds of Big O answers.

Instead, learn to **look at code and count how the work scales with `n`**.

A solid progression for DSA would be:

blocks.code:
O(1)
 ↓
O(n)
 ↓
O(n²)
 ↓
O(log n)
 ↓
O(n log n)
 ↓
Recursion
 ↓
Space complexity
 ↓
Data structure operation complexities

blocks.body: Once you can look at a piece of JavaScript and immediately say **"one loop = O(n), nested loops = O(n²), halving = O(log n)"**, you're ready to tackle a large chunk of the Big O questions that appear in DSA tests.
